entries.title: About the Course
entries.content:
Journey into the 19th century via novels, short stories, personal narratives, fairy tales, and more. Students engage with a variety of authors and texts from and about the time period and reflect on literary techniques and the characteristics of multiple genres along the way.

This topic is included in the following course(s): Literature: Grade 11, Literature: Grade 12

entries.title: Placement & Combining Tips
entries.content: Some books shared with other high school grades. Literature, history, and geography lessons work in sync in Grades 9-12, so it is best to consider all three together when placing students.

General Lit.: Grades 11-12
Jane Eyre (Term 2: Option 1) This novel touches on difficult themes including a child in an unhappy home situation, loss, a romantic relationship with a significant secret, mental illness, and questions of faith and duty. Teachers may wish to preview these elements before assigning.

James (Term 2: Option 2) This novel is recommended for mature students, as it includes strong language, racial slurs and stereotypes, and graphic scenes of violence and abuse, mainly directed towards the enslaved characters in the novel. Pre-reading or familiarizing yourself with the content to determine suitability for your student(s) is encouraged.

books.title: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass

blocks.text: The lesson plans will guide you through what to read over the terms. Take a moment before reading to remember where you left off last time.
The lesson plans will give you specific instructions or tell you to choose a way to narrate that helps you interact with the ideas.
The lesson plans will guide you with questions or instructions to share your ideas or what you are reading with others.

These lessons are written directly to students, but to assist them throughout the year, please read through this section and the lesson plans so you are familiar with the instructions and flow of the lessons. Accountability components are occasionally added to facilitate teacher/student discussion and growing independence. 

It is also valuable for those in a classroom setting to have a mix of lessons that students complete themselves silently and others read aloud and narrate together. Literature lessons lend themselves well to a larger discussion time at the end of the lesson where student can share their ideas.

lessons.title: 30m General Lit.: Grades 11-12 - Lesson 25
lessons.body:
⍞ Materials: Jane Eyre OR James

➜ INTRO (Option 1: Jane Eyre)
Orient yourself a bit more to Jane Eyre.

➜ READ 
p. 3 "Introduction to the Author" and p. 10 "Background of the Work" 
p. 32-39 Chapter 1

Note: This book is too long to finish in the term just by reading during lesson time. Feel free to read more of the book in your free time or, if you are interested, you can finish the book after the end of the term.   

➜ NARRATE, & DISCUSS
Write, sketch, or tell your narration briefly and then save 5-10 minutes to either answer the question(s) below or pick a few reflection questions of your own at the end of each chapter to discuss (orally or in writing).

• The first sentence of this novel is the famous: "There was no possibility of taking a walk that day." What is evoked by this sentence? What does it assume, deny, allude to? 

• View question #2 or #3  on page 263 and reflect orally or in writing, 
---------------

➜ INTRO (Option 2: James)

Note: This book is too long to finish in the term just by reading during lesson time. Feel free to read more of the book in your free time or, if you are interested, you can finish the book after the end of the term.   

➜ READ p.9-20 Chapter 1

➜ READ
Huckleberry Finn Chapter 2 opening scene

➜ NARRATE, & DISCUSS
• What do you notice reading these two scenes back to back? How does Percival Everett reimagine the scene from Huckleberry Finn? Which details does he keep and what does he change? What is the overall affect?

⍞ Materials: Jane Eyre OR James

How was Jane's "nature" (her personality) portrayed in chapter one and what role does it have in the plot so far? 

➜ INTRO (Option 1: Jane Eyre)

Keep the idea of the quest in mind in reading the novel. What is Jane's quest? What is she looking for? Is what she wants the same as what she needs?

---------------

➜ RECAP (Option 2: James)
What are your first impressions of the character of Jim?

➜ READ, NARRATE, & DISCUSS

• p. 21-32  Chapters 2-3
What do you learn about language in this section? How does it contribute to the irony of the novel?
What is the first interaction like between James and Huck?

➜ VIEW
Understanding Everett's aims and vision for James as you begin the novel will serve as a helpful guide as you read through it.
Giving "James" a Voice: Percival Everett on his Reimagining of Huck Finn
lessons.teacherNotes:
COMPOSITION PROMPT

How does the scene in the red room reflect Gothic literature? (Elements of Gothic literature include mystery, death, the supernatural, gloom and doom, and horror.) Notice details such as the secret drawer in the wardrobe, the jewel-casket, and parchment, along with words such as spell, secret, blood, and chill. Does the scene become too unrealistic to be believable, or does Bronte suceed in making it realistic?

lessons.title: 30m General Lit.: Grades 11-12 - Lesson 43
lessons.body:
⍞ Materials: Jane Eyre OR James

➜ RECAP (Option 1: Jane Eyre)

• How did Jane meet Mr. Rochester? 

➜ READ, NARRATE, & DISCUSS

• p. 209-244 Chapter 13 & 14 This week is a longer reading. You can split this lesson between two days this week, read some in your free time, OR read/listen for about 20 minutes and narrate for 10 minutes. 

➜ NARRATE, & DISCUSS
Write, sketch, or tell your narration briefly and then save 5-10 minutes to either answer the question(s) below or pick a few reflection questions of your own at the end of each chapter to discuss (orally or in writing).

• Why do you think Brontë introduces Rochester as someone who breaks the rules of polite behavior? How does Jane's refusal to defer to him set up their relationship as something different from the typical governess-employer dynamic?

Do you find Rochester sympathetic at this point in the novel, or does something about him make you uneasy? 

➜ RECAP (Option 2: James)

➜ READ, NARRATE, & DISCUSS

• p.170-196 Ch.30-Part 2 Ch.1
